description: Solo team. I am an architecture student from Minsk with an interest in space architecture. My project, Long Shadows, is a site-planning tool for a base at the Moon's south pole: it compares landing sites and dates by sunlight and line to Earth, and lets you place solar masts and antennas on real NASA terrain to see how they shade each other.
summary:
Long Shadows answers the question that comes after "where is it sunny?": how to lay out a base there. At the Moon's south pole the Sun never climbs above 1.6°, so a 10 m solar mast casts a shadow longer than 350 m. You place masts and antennas on real NASA terrain and see which mast shades which and what blocks the line to Earth; a rover route goes round the shadows that would empty its battery.
 
To choose the site and the date first, the tool does what the challenge asks. For 18 landing sites, and for any point you click, it shows the Sun and Earth moving over the real skyline measured by NASA's LOLA altimeter. It gives a verdict for the chosen landing date (hours of sunlight, Earth in view, ground slope, nearest permanent shadow) and compares sites and dates side by side.
 
Every figure is checked: Sun and Earth directions against JPL Horizons (0.0007°), sunlight against NASA's illumination maps (1.3 points on average). Two modes share the same calculations: Standard explains in plain words for teachers and the public, Advanced gives mission planners tables of exact figures with their sources.
details:
WHAT IS NEW

Many tools show sunlight at the pole. Long Shadows adds the layout of a base, the way an architect plans a site: several masts and antennas on real terrain, their shadows on each other over a lunar day, and a rover that has to live through those shadows.

WHAT IT DOES

A web tool with five screens. A seven-step tour on the first screen walks through all of it in a minute; a second button leads straight to the base plan.

1. Map. Eighteen sites near the south pole: NASA's nine Artemis III candidate regions, commercial landers, real landings. Layers of average sunlight, Earth visibility and relief. Click anywhere to analyse a point of your own.

2. Horizon. The real skyline of the site with the Sun and Earth travelling along it, for any hour from August 2023 to December 2028. A verdict for a landing at the chosen moment, a countdown to sunset and Earthset, a calendar of landing dates, and replays of five real landings.

3. Compare. Three sites on one date, or one site on three dates, to see what a slipped launch costs.

4. Base plan. Solar masts and antennas placed on real terrain in a 4 km box. The checks show which mast shades which and what blocks the line to Earth. A rover route goes round the shadows that would empty its battery.

5. About. Checks against NASA data, glossary, limits and sources.

TWO MODES

A switch in the header changes the depth, not the calculations. Standard explains: a verdict in plain words, notes on the pictures, the few figures that matter most. Advanced is the working tool: the verdict as a table of exact figures with the source of each, all sites in one sortable table, CSV files of everything, slope at lander scale from NASA's 5 m site maps, which Deep Space Network complex has the Moon in its sky at each hour, surface temperature and buried-ice depth from LRO Diviner maps, a list of your own points, the base plan on two more sites.

HOW IT WORKS

Python scripts read NASA's LOLA elevation maps and trace the skyline of every site in 720 directions out to 320 km, at 2, 10 and 20 m above the ground. The directions to the Sun and Earth come from the JPL DE421 ephemeris, hour by hour, in the same Moon-fixed frame the LOLA maps use, with libration and the aberration of sunlight. The browser then compares two things: where the Sun or Earth is, and how high the skyline is in that direction. The site is static: plain JavaScript without a framework, three.js for the two 3D views, no server.

HOW WE KNOW IT IS RIGHT

- Sun and Earth directions against JPL Horizons: largest gap 0.0007°.

- Sunlight against NASA's LOLA illumination maps at 15 sites: 1.3 percentage points on average, correlation 0.99.

- Ground slope at the IM-1 landing site: 11.5° here, 12° reported by the LRO camera team.

- Rover lighting rule against the full calculation: the same answer in 99.75% of 1,059,960 cell-hours.

- 84 automatic checks run in a headless browser with one command and on GitHub at every push. Accessibility checked with axe-core (WCAG 2.1 A and AA): no issues left.

WHO IT IS FOR, AND ITS LIMITS

Mission planners get exact numbers, CSV export and links that restore a view. Teachers and the public get plain words, a glossary and replays of landings they have heard of. It is a tool for quick comparison of sites and dates and for teaching, not a mission design tool: terrain is as fine as LOLA (5 to 240 m per pixel), rocks and small craters are not seen, and energy figures are rough.

TOOLS

JavaScript, HTML and CSS; Python (NumPy, SciPy) for the data; three.js; Playwright and axe-core for the tests; GitHub Pages.

Code, tests and a judge guide: https://github.com/hvozdzvera/long-shadows

USE OF Super Intelligence (SI)

I, Vera Hvozdz, was responsible for the idea, the product design, the UX and interface design, setting the tasks for the calculations, QA testing and deployment. The calculation algorithms, the code and the automatic checks were written with an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) under my direction. The demo video is a screen recording of the live site, made with the same assistant. No AI-generated images and no AI-generated data: every figure is computed from the NASA data listed below. The use of AI is also stated on the About screen of the site, in the README, in the page metadata and at the top of every code file.
dataRefs: LRO LOLA Gridded Data Records, polar elevation maps (LDEM) and average Sun and Earth visibility maps (AVGVISIB)
High-Resolution LOLA Topography for Lunar South Pole Sites, 5 m (NASA GSFC PGDA)
JPL planetary and lunar ephemeris DE421
LRO Diviner polar maps of temperature and ice stability (Schorghofer & Williams 2020)
projectRefs: USGS: Down Selected Artemis III Candidate Landing Site Navigational Grids
Firefly Aerospace: Blue Ghost Mission 1 facts
Intuitive Machines: IM-1 and IM-2 facts
Astropy, used for one independent check (BSD licence)
B612 and B612 Mono fonts (SIL Open Font License)
Claude (Anthropic), AI assistant used to write the code
